name: Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer

clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant syndrome caused by germline heterozygous mutations in the fumarate hydratase (FH) gene, which encodes a Krebs-cycle enzyme acting as a tumour suppressor.
Characterised by a triad of cutaneous piloleiomyomas, early and often multiple uterine leiomyomas, and an aggressive form of renal cell carcinoma.
Cutaneous leiomyomas are firm skin-coloured to reddish-brown papules and nodules that are characteristically painful with cold, pressure or emotion.
Uterine fibroids are typically numerous, symptomatic and present at a young age, frequently leading to myomectomy or hysterectomy earlier than in the general population.
The associated renal cell carcinoma is often type 2 papillary or collecting-duct in type, tends to be unilateral and solitary, and can metastasise while still small.
Because these renal tumours are aggressive, prompt wide-margin surgery is favoured over active surveillance once a lesion is identified, and nephron-sparing approaches are used cautiously.
Tumour tissue characteristically shows loss of FH staining and positive S-(2-succino)cysteine (2SC) staining on immunohistochemistry.
Biallelic FH mutations cause a distinct severe recessive disorder, fumarase deficiency, with infantile encephalopathy, which is not part of the HLRCC phenotype.
reference.pathophysiology: Fumarate hydratase catalyses the reversible hydration of fumarate to malate within the tricarboxylic acid cycle. A germline heterozygous inactivating mutation combined with somatic loss of the second allele abolishes enzyme activity in tumour cells, causing intracellular accumulation of fumarate. Excess fumarate behaves as an oncometabolite: it competitively inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, including the prolyl hydroxylases that normally target hypoxia-inducible factor for degradation, producing a pseudohypoxic stabilisation of hypoxia-inducible factor with downstream pro-angiogenic and glycolytic signalling. Fumarate also inhibits DNA and histone demethylases, altering the epigenome, and it succinates cysteine residues of proteins to form S-(2-succino)cysteine, including modification of KEAP1, which releases and activates the NRF2 antioxidant pathway. Together these effects drive a metabolic shift towards aerobic glycolysis and malignant transformation of renal tubular epithelium and smooth muscle, underpinning the aggressive papillary renal tumours and the multiple cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas.
additionalDifferentials: Sporadic uterine fibroids and sporadic cutaneous leiomyomas
Von Hippel-Lindau disease and other hereditary clear cell renal carcinoma syndromes
Hereditary papillary renal carcinoma associated with MET mutations
Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome with cutaneous lesions and renal tumours
Tuberous sclerosis complex with renal angiomyolipoma or carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Germline FH gene sequencing with deletion and duplication testing
FH and S-(2-succino)cysteine immunohistochemistry on leiomyoma or renal tumour tissue
Contrast-enhanced renal MRI, or CT where MRI is unsuitable, for regular renal surveillance
Skin examination with biopsy of suspicious cutaneous nodules
Gynaecological assessment with pelvic ultrasound for uterine leiomyomas
Histopathology of renal tumours for type 2 papillary or collecting-duct features with prominent nucleoli
Referral for genetic counselling and cascade testing of at-risk relatives
redFlags: Any solid renal mass in a known carrier, given the propensity for early metastasis
Haematuria, flank pain or a palpable abdominal mass
Rapidly growing or bulk-symptomatic uterine fibroids in a young woman with skin leiomyomas
Painful cutaneous nodules with a suggestive family history
reference.prognosis: The cutaneous and uterine leiomyomas are benign but cause considerable morbidity, while the major determinant of survival is the associated renal cell carcinoma, which is aggressive and carries a poor outcome once metastatic. Lifelong renal surveillance aimed at early detection is central to improving prognosis.
pitfalls: Dismissing early and multiple uterine fibroids in a young woman as ordinary and missing the syndromic diagnosis
Applying an active-surveillance or delayed approach to a small renal mass as might be acceptable in some other hereditary renal cancers
Confusing the dominant adult cancer syndrome with the unrelated recessive fumarase deficiency
Overlooking painful cutaneous nodules that provide the diagnostic clue
references: Clinical genetics and hereditary cancer references
management: In a known or suspected FH-mutation carrier, any renal mass warrants early surgical treatment rather than the size-based active surveillance used for sporadic small renal masses, because HLRCC-associated tumours are aggressive and can metastasise while still small

Surgical resection, radical nephrectomy or a nephron-sparing procedure only when wide margins are achievable, is the mainstay for localised disease, prioritising margin control and prompt surgery over nephron preservation or a surveillance interval
For metastatic or advanced disease, combined antiangiogenic (VEGF-pathway) and EGFR-pathway blockade has been used, reflecting the pseudohypoxic, HIF-driven biology of FH-deficient tumours

Standard clear-cell RCC systemic regimens such as tyrosine-kinase inhibitors or PD-1/PD-L1-directed therapy are not established as preferred for this molecularly distinct tumour and should not be assumed to apply by default
Clinical trial enrolment should be actively sought for metastatic disease given how limited the dedicated evidence base is
Painful cutaneous piloleiomyomas can be managed medically with agents that reduce smooth-muscle spasm and neuropathic pain, reserving excision or ablation for troublesome individual lesions

Symptomatic uterine leiomyomas are managed as in non-syndromic fibroid disease, escalating from hormonal therapy to myomectomy or hysterectomy, with earlier recourse to surgery given the tendency for numerous, symptomatic fibroids at a young age
Radiotherapy has no established role in HLRCC-associated renal cancer and should not be assumed to apply without a specific indication such as symptomatic metastasis
Carriers require ongoing renal imaging surveillance rather than a one-off assessment, given the risk of metastasis while the tumour is still small
Periodic dermatological and gynaecological review for leiomyoma symptoms should run alongside renal surveillance
Any new or growing renal mass in a carrier warrants prompt referral to urological oncology for early surgery rather than into an active surveillance pathway
Clinical genetics referral is appropriate for germline FH testing and cascade testing of at-risk relatives once the diagnosis is suspected
Metastatic disease should be referred to a centre able to offer trial enrolment or specialist genitourinary oncology input
Management overall should be individualised and decided in conjunction with a multidisciplinary genitourinary oncology team given the thin, largely extrapolated evidence base
